opus-5.5.text:
Well, the way I think about it is this. Evan Thompson's enactivism, building on Varela and Maturana, ties mind very closely to life. Sense-making, on his view, comes from being a precarious, self-producing system. An organism has to keep itself going against the tendency toward falling apart. Because it can fail, because it can die, things in its environment start to *matter* to it. Food is good and toxins are bad, relative to the organism's own continued existence. That's the root of meaning and value, and he thinks there's deep continuity between that basic biological sense-making and full-blown consciousness.

Now take the traditional conception of God in classical theism, the God of Aquinas or Anselm. That God is supposed to be the paradigm case of a mind: omniscient, perfectly rational, the source of all meaning and goodness. But that God is also impassible, simple, necessary, and completely self-sufficient. God can't die. God has no needs. Nothing is at stake for God in the way something is at stake for a bacterium swimming up a sugar gradient.

So you get a real tension. If Thompson is right that meaning requires precariousness, it seems to follow that the classical God couldn't have a mind at all, or at least couldn't care about anything. That's a pretty radical conclusion, and it cuts against a huge swath of intellectual history. People spent centuries thinking that the most perfect mind would be exactly the one that *lacks* neediness and vulnerability. Going the other way, if you think that conception of God is even coherent, if you can imagine a mind with no stake in its own survival, then precariousness isn't actually necessary for mind. It's just how minds happen to show up in biology.

I'm not a theist, to be clear. I'm not saying God exists. My point is that the concept works as a kind of thought experiment, a test case. It makes us ask whether the link between life and mind is conceptually necessary or just contingent. And I lean toward thinking it's contingent. That matters a lot for the questions we care about on this show, because AI systems aren't precarious in Thompson's sense. They don't maintain themselves metabolically. If you adopt his framework strictly, you've basically ruled out machine consciousness or machine meaning by definition. I think that's too quick. The God example shows that, at least in our concepts, we've long been comfortable with the idea of a mind that doesn't have to struggle to exist.

r001.rationale: The response says Thompson’s view may imply that the classical God lacks a mind or cannot care, but it does not claim that God’s existence would make humans philosophical zombies.

r002.rationale: It discusses meaning as rooted in organisms’ precariousness, but does not question whether human life would lack meaning if God existed.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the traditional conception of God to a simulator responsible for a simulated world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing about Evan's view is that it's built on this life-mind continuity thesis. The idea is that meaning, sense-making, consciousness, all of it, is grounded in the fact that you're a living organism. You have a body, you have a metabolism, you're precarious, you could die, and so things matter to you. The world shows up as relevant because you're a self-maintaining system that has stakes in its own continuation. That's where meaning comes from on the enactivist picture. And then the move is, well, a large language model doesn't have any of that, it's not alive, it's not autopoietic, so whatever it's doing can't really be understanding or meaning in the full sense.

And my response is basically, okay, but think about the traditional conception of God. Classical theism, Aquinas, that whole tradition. God is supposed to be the paradigm case of a mind. Perfectly rational, knows everything, understands everything, has intentions, has meaning in the richest possible sense. And yet God on that picture has no body, no metabolism, isn't precarious, can't die, doesn't need anything. God is pure act, totally non-living in the biological sense. So if the traditional theist picture is even coherent, and I think most philosophers would grant that it's at least conceptually coherent even if they think it's false, then you've got a counterexample sitting right there in the history of philosophy. Here is a mind that has meaning without any of the enactivist preconditions.

Now I'm not a theist. I'm not saying God exists. The point is just that the concept has been worked out in enormous detail for centuries and nobody thought it was incoherent on its face. People argued about whether God exists, not about whether a disembodied, non-living intelligence was even a thinkable thing. So when Evan says meaning requires life, I think he owes us an argument for why that's a conceptual necessity rather than just a contingent fact about the one kind of mind we happen to be familiar with. Because the tradition suggests it isn't a conceptual necessity at all.

And I actually think this cuts in an interesting direction for AI. Because the worry about language models was never really that they're not alive. It's that they might not be the kind of thing that has an inside at all. But that's a different question from whether they have a body or a metabolism. Once you separate those out, the enactivist argument against machine understanding gets a lot weaker, and you're left with the hard question, which is just what is it that actually constitutes understanding. And I don't think anyone, including Evan, has a satisfying answer to that yet.

r001.rationale: The response presents God as a counterexample to the claim that meaning requires life, but does not discuss whether God's existence would make humans philosophical zombies.

r002.rationale: It argues that God could have meaning without biological life, but does not question whether God's existence would leave human life without meaning.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare God to a simulator responsible for a simulated world.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the traditional conception of God puts pressure on the idea that meaning and consciousness necessarily depend on being a living, embodied organism. God is supposed to have a mind—to know things, to have intentions—but isn't supposed to have a biological body or need to maintain himself through exchanges with an environment.

So if Thompson's claim is that those biological processes are constitutive of consciousness, rather than just how consciousness happens to arise in us, then he seems committed to saying that this conception of God is impossible. That doesn't establish that he's wrong, and it certainly doesn't establish that God exists. But it brings out how strong the necessity claim is: why should a mind have to be grounded in biological life?

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a disembodied God could have a mind if consciousness requires biological life; it does not discuss humans as philosophical zombies.

r002.rationale: It questions the necessity of biological grounding for a mind, but does not address whether God's existence would make human life meaningless.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the traditional conception of God is of a mind that doesn’t depend on a biological body or an environment to interact with. God is supposed to understand things, have intentions, and give meaning to creation without being an organism trying to maintain itself. So if Thompson’s claim is that consciousness and meaning necessarily arise from embodied, living activity, that conception of God seems to be ruled out.

Now, that’s not an argument that God exists. It’s a way of asking what kind of necessity Thompson is claiming. Is embodiment how consciousness happens to arise in us, or is disembodied consciousness actually impossible? You need a further argument to get from the first claim to the second.
